title: Git push get an AI API: Ryan Fox-Tyler

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is the Hypermode developer platform—providing model hosting, auto-generated GraphQL, git-push deployment, and observability for engineers building AI systems. Hypermode is explicitly a developer platform for software builders, and the workshop demonstrates AI features across multiple use cases without being tied to a specific vertical. The workshop covers writing and building AI functions, deploying via git push, and observing model behavior through inference history and logs. Attendees need Node.js, Git, and a text editor, but the workshop provides step-by-step guidance, templates, and live demos. Hands-on workshop with audience participation, code walkthroughs, and live demonstrations at the AI Engineer World's Fair. Multiple evidence anchors are directly sourced from the transcript with specific character offsets.

summary: The workshop opens with Ryan Fox-Tyler introducing Hypermode's philosophy that iteration is everything in AI development. The audience plays "Hyper Categories," a scaled-up Scattergories game where players submit unique category entries. Behind the scenes, the game validates answers using models and dictionary checks, and clusters responses via similarity search. Fox-Tyler frames AI applications as building blocks: functions, models, and data sources. The workshop transitions to GitHub issue triage—using AI to classify issues, find similar ones, summarize trends, and detect outliers. Attendees deploy a template from justship.ai, connect GitHub, clone the repo, run npm install, and build the project. The starter template contains two functions: classifyIssue and trendSummary. Hypermode uses AssemblyScript, a TypeScript-like language compiling to WebAssembly. Fox-Tyler walks through trendSummary, which fetches issues from GitHub via REST API, constructs a prompt, and sends it to OpenAI's GPT-4. Hypermode's strongly typed model interface provides IntelliSense for model parameters, abstracting provider differences. Deployment is as simple as git commit and git push, auto-generating a GraphQL schema from exported functions. The Hypermode console provides an inferences tab showing model run history with timing, inputs, outputs, and token consumption, plus raw function logs and a deployments tab linking to git commits. Fox-Tyler then walks through classifyIssue, which uses a small purpose-built HuggingFace model pre-trained on GitHub issues to classify entries as bug, feature request, question, or issue. This model gets automatically provisioned as a dedicated instance within Hypermode. The final segment builds natural language search: Fox-Tyler adds a MiniLM embeddings model from sentence-transformers to hypermode.json, creates an embedder function that returns flat32 vector arrays, and a search function that queries a Hypermode collection for similar issues. He pre-seeds the collection with a CSV of GitHub issues from the Transformers repo, and the platform automatically embeds all uploaded data using the configured embedder function. A live search for a Spanish README issue returns related issues (Turkish README, French version) with correct similarity matching. He notes that structured objects work as return types (generating GraphQL types), that functions must be explicitly exported from the index file to be included in the build, and that local dev experience is still being improved. Fox-Tyler closes by mentioning upcoming PostgreSQL connectivity, 14-day trials for attendees, and claimable credits.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & Agenda
sections.summary: Ryan introduces Hypermode's iteration philosophy, outlines the workshop agenda, and previews the Hyper Categories game format.

sections.title: Hyper Categories Game
sections.summary: Audience plays Hyper Categories via QR code with the letter T. A bot competes but picks obvious answers and finishes fourth. Kirk Bui and Francisco tie for first, each winning a jacket.

sections.title: Behind the Scenes: Building Blocks
sections.summary: Breakdown of game architecture: model-based category validation, dictionary validation added after model accepted 'P doctor', similarity-based clustering for scoring, and the framing of AI apps as functions, models, and data sources.

sections.title: GitHub Issue Triage Introduction
sections.summary: Transition to applying AI concepts to GitHub issue triage for classification, finding similar issues, summarizing trends, and detecting outliers using open data.

sections.title: Workshop Setup & Template Deployment
sections.summary: Attendees deploy the GitHub issue triage template from justship.ai, connect their GitHub account, clone the repo, and open it in VS Code. Prerequisites: Node.js 20+, Git. Section pauses for attendees to clone the starter template.

sections.title: Installing Dependencies & Building the Project
sections.summary: Fox-Tyler walks through npm install in the functions directory, addressing a VS Code TypeScript language server quirk causing red squiggles. Clarifies that deploying via justship.ai creates the Hypermode org automatically. Running npm run build shows ASCII art and metadata for two functions: classifyIssue and trendSummary.

sections.title: AssemblyScript & Hypermode Execution Model
sections.summary: Explains that Hypermode functions are written in AssemblyScript, a TypeScript-like language that compiles to WebAssembly for secure, performant execution. Other language support is planned for the future.

sections.title: trendSummary Function Walkthrough
sections.summary: Walks through the trendSummary function: a helper fetches issues from GitHub via REST API with secrets management for tokens, constructs a prompt asking GPT-4 to summarize trends, and uses Hypermode's strongly typed OpenAI chat model interface with IntelliSense for parameters like temperature and topP. Emphasizes models are not interchangeable across providers. Developers can write custom model interfaces by inheriting from a base class.

sections.title: Deployment & Live Demo
sections.summary: Git commit and push automatically deploys to the Hypermode console. Hypermode auto-generates a GraphQL schema from exported functions. Fox-Tyler demonstrates live by running trendSummary against the dotnet/runtime repository, fetching the top 100 issues and receiving a trend summary within seconds via the built-in GraphQL query tab.

sections.title: GraphQL Type Generation & Observability
sections.summary: Fox-Tyler confirms Hypermode auto-generates GraphQL types from TypeScript types, including custom scalars. Current limitation: input types must be scalars or arrays; structured objects as inputs require future engineering. He shows the inferences tab with model run history (timing, inputs, outputs, token consumption even when unused in code), raw function logs oriented per execution, and a deployments tab linking to git commits for change tracking.

sections.title: classifyIssue Function & HuggingFace Model
sections.summary: Introduces classifyIssue, which takes title, description, and issue ID as inputs and uses a small purpose-built HuggingFace model ('thebert mnli GitHub issues') pre-trained on GitHub issues to classify as bug, feature request, question, or issue. The model is imported from an experimental classification models library, supports batch inputs, and returns confidence scores. Fox-Tyler notes that deploying this project automatically provisions a dedicated instance of the model within Hypermode, contrasting with external OpenAI models.

sections.title: classifyIssue Live Demo & Confidence Thresholds
sections.summary: Live demo of classifyIssue via GraphQL query. The example query from docs had escaping issues with newlines and quotes; Fox-Tyler works around this. The model classifies the input as a real issue. He mentions a docs walkthrough for adding confidence score thresholds—pure code, no model retraining needed—but skips hands-on implementation due to time constraints.

sections.title: Natural Language Search Setup
sections.summary: Fox-Tyler begins building a natural language search feature to identify similar GitHub issues, envisioning a bot that tells users their issue resembles existing ones. He introduces Hypermode collections—an in-memory key-value store with vector indexing—and configures one in the hypermode.json manifest file alongside existing models and hosts definitions.

sections.title: Natural Language Search Implementation
sections.summary: Fox-Tyler adds a MiniLM embeddings model from sentence-transformers to hypermode.json, hosted on Hypermode and sourced from HuggingFace. He git pushes to start provisioning the model. He then creates an embedder function that takes text in and returns flat32 vector arrays, and a search function that queries the collection for the top three similar issues with text included in results. Both functions must be explicitly exported from the index file to be included in the build. He confirms structured objects work as return types, auto-generating GraphQL types. The search function is deployed via git push.

sections.title: Natural Language Search Demo & Wrap-up
sections.summary: Fox-Tyler pre-seeds the collection by uploading a CSV of GitHub issues scraped from the Transformers repo. Hypermode automatically embeds all uploaded data using the configured embedder function. A live search for a Spanish README issue returns similar issues (Turkish README, French version) with correct similarity matching, though inference logs were slow to appear. Batch embeddings were split into 25-item chunks taking 1-2 seconds each. Fox-Tyler wraps up by mentioning upcoming PostgreSQL connectivity, 14-day trials for attendees, claimable credits from Kevin's morning talk, and additional documentation covering HTTP calls and collections. He emphasizes these building blocks—functions, models, data sources—can be applied across many application contexts.
